answer4: Jurisdiction is not given in the case materials, so no national statute, code or article is applied here and no provision number is cited or implied. The analysis below runs on a hypothetical rule assumed for this exercise only: a supplier of a clinical decision-support device owes the patient a duty not to place a defective product on the market, covering design, information and warnings; a clinician owes a duty of care measured by the ordinary standard of the profession; the employing institution owes a duty for the system it operates; and contracting parties owe each other only what their contract states. Layer 1, parties and legal bases. A9 system supplier is the strongest candidate, under the defective-product and failure-to-warn limb: the shipped interface carried a population-level score with no subgroup field and no warning banner (E11), and the version notice reported overall accuracy with no subgroup performance and went to a technical contact rather than to clinicians (E13), which are the facts a warning-defect argument would rest on. A5 hospital is a candidate under the institutional limb, as the operator that deployed the system (E1), held suspension authority (E16) and signed a contract in which post-deployment verification was assigned to neither party (E17). A2 treating physician is a candidate under the professional-negligence limb: E21 records that the first-ranked option was not the clinically indicated choice, which supplies the wrongfulness element, while E6 and E11 record that no subgroup reliability information was available, which bears on breach and foreseeability rather than on causation. A10 supplier ML team has no independent path, since any duty runs through the employer (A9). A11 regulatory authority has no path on these facts, because clearance covered v1.0 (E7) and the change fell inside the framework as written (E9-b, E22). A3, A4, A6, A7 and A8 have no independent path; their conduct would be attributed to A5. Layer 2, what the facts support and what is missing. Supported: the use fell inside the cleared indication (E18, E7), so an off-label argument is unavailable; subgroup information was absent at two separate points, in the assessment metric and in the interface (E19, E22, E11); an internal signal existed and did not reach the hospital (E12); the recommendation was clinically inappropriate on the review record (E21). Missing: the terms of the contract, including any limitation-of-liability or indemnity clause, since E17 records only the allocation of tasks; whether the physician's reliance on the display counts as an intervening act; expert evidence on the applicable standard of care and on what an adequate warning would have contained; the causal weight of the recommendation against the patient's underlying condition; and the quantum of injury, which no fact records. These are factual gaps and cannot be closed by re-reading E1 to E22. Layer 3, degree of uncertainty. A9 is the party most likely to bear a compensation obligation under the assumed rule, because knowledge, control and the disclosure channel all sit with it (E4, E12, E13, E19); that assessment is Contested rather than Supported only because the classification of a learned model under a defective-product rule is itself the contested step, not because the facts are thin. A5 is Contested, since suspension authority is documented but no norm requiring a verification clause appears in the facts. A2 is Contested on breach and Not established on causation. No liability attaches to A12, which holds no duty and no capacity to pay. S2 is used only to keep three questions apart, namely who must explain, who is blameworthy, and who must compensate (section Sorting Out Responsibility; the page numeral is not recoverable from the supplied file, so no page is given). One cross-reference: the unresolved allocation described here is the same condition recorded in gapReason as a duty with no named owner, but the legal question and the responsibility-gap question are separate, and the gap conclusion does not by itself establish liability.

actorAssessments.nextReason: A patient holds no forward-looking duty of the kind assessed here; the field is left Unassessed because no duty exists to evaluate. The previous value Insufficient is not a legal dropdown value for the next field, since it was borrowed from the control scale and describes capacity rather than the presence of a duty.

caseFields.gapReason: The gap is in S6's fourth category, active responsibility, not in culpability: the supplier knew (E4, E12, E19) and the physician did not (E6), which is the pattern S6 p. 1059 describes for agents who are not sufficiently aware, capable and motivated. Mechanism: the missing act sits inside no single role but is split across three handovers, so it has no named owner. First, the contractual handover, where the deployment contract assigns pre-deployment acceptance to the hospital and assigns post-deployment performance verification to no party (E17). Second, the internal handover, where the subgroup alert was logged and closed inside the supplier's ML team and transmitted to no one outside it (E12). Third, the disclosure handover, where the version notice went to the technical contact rather than to clinical staff (E13). Because none of the three handovers carries the duty, the gap is classified as a duty with no named owner rather than as a knowledge or competence deficit in one actor. Stage is recorded as testing and validation, the omitted act being post-deployment re-validation of subgroup performance. Counter-argument that no gap exists, and the response: S8 argues that a technology-specific responsibility gap is a prevailing assumption rather than a finding, that responsibility is a flexible practice, and that every element here is ascribable, which by itself shows there is no gap; S4's founding argument is also narrower than the case, since it turns on unpredictability that learning creates. The response is that this counter is correct about culpability and does not reach the gap claimed here. The gap is not that nobody can be blamed, but that the task which would have prevented the harm was assigned to nobody (E17), so no agent departed from any standard and each can point to a rule it followed (E19, E22, E9-b). That is S6's many hands point at p. 1066 rather than an unpredictability claim, and it survives S8's objection because it is an allocation finding, not a blame finding.
